name: Ottoman Millet System, Religious Community Governance
summary: Following the conquest of Constantinople, Mehmed II formalizes the Ottoman millet system, allowing non-Muslim communities (Greek Orthodox, Armenian Apostolic, Jewish) to govern themselves according to their own religious laws in personal status matters (marriage, inheritance, religious courts) while paying a special tax (jizya). The Patriarch of Constantinople is recognized as the head (ethnarch) of the Rum Millet.

_quarry.structural_significance: The millet system is the Ottoman solution to governing a multi-religious empire; it preserves non-Muslim institutions while ensuring tax extraction and political subordination; the system's relative tolerance (compared to Western Christendom's treatment of religious minorities) makes the Ottoman Empire a refuge for Spanish Jews expelled in 1492; the millet institutions become the foundation for the communal organizations that survive into the modern states of the Balkans and Middle East
